title: Greetings and introductions
goal: Greet people, introduce yourself and say goodbye with the words Malaysians really use — while picking up two sound habits that will change how you hear the whole language.
bekal: greet people by time of day and by how well you know them, including the safest greeting of all
introduce yourself and ask back without sounding like you're filling in a form
use the particle *-lah*, a softener English has no single word for

dialogs.title: Dialogue — At the residential college
dialogs.intro: Sarah's first day at a University of Malaya residential college. She is dragging her bag down the corridor when a student comes out of the kitchen holding a cup.

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.id: Hi! Are you the new girl?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ya, saya baru sampai. Nama saya Sarah.
lines.id: Yes, I've just arrived. My name is Sarah.
lines.literal: yes, I just arrive. name I Sarah.

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Saya Aina. Selamat datang! Apa khabar?
lines.id: I'm Aina. Welcome! How are you?
lines.literal: I Aina. safe arrive! what news?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: I'm fine, just a bit tired.

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.id: Of course you're tired. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Oh, patutlah pelat awak lain sikit. Saya orang Kelantan.
lines.id: Oh, that explains why your accent is a bit different. I'm from Kelantan.
lines.literal: oh, fitting-lah accent you different little. I person Kelantan.

lines.speaker: Aina:
lines.text: Jauh juga. Lapan jam naik bas. Bilik awak nombor berapa?
lines.id: Pretty far. Eight hours by bus. What's your room number?
lines.literal: far also. eight hour ride bus. room you number how-many?

lines.id: You're welcome. See you later, OK?

notes: **Apa khabar?** — the most common greeting, literally "what news?". The answer is almost always **khabar baik** ("news good" = I'm fine). Casually people also say *apa cerita?* ("what's the story?") or, among young people, *okay tak?* If you've met Indonesian: it spells this word *kabar*, without the *h*.

**Budak** means **child, kid, youngster**. *Budak baru* here means "the new kid", and *budak-budak* means "children". You'll hear it constantly: *budak sekolah* (schoolkid), *budak kolej* (college kid), *budak lelaki* (boy). ⚠️ In Indonesian *budak* means "slave" — one of many false friends between the two languages.

**Ke** at the end of a sentence is the **conversational question marker** — like a rising "…, right?" or "…, is it?" in English. *Awak budak baru ke?* = "Are you the new kid?" The formal version is *-kah* (*Adakah awak pelajar baru?*), but in conversation almost everyone uses *ke*. Note its position: always at the **end** of the sentence.
**Penat** means **tired** — far more common than the formal *letih*. **Sikit** is the spoken form of *sedikit* (a little), shortened the way English turns "going to" into "gonna".

**Beg** = bag, **bilik** = room, **tandas** = toilet, **bas** = bus, **nombor** = number. Notice the pattern: Malay borrowed heavily from English, so *beg*, *bas* and *nombor* will look familiar once you say them aloud. Malay spelling simply writes English words the way they sound to a Malay ear.

grammars.title: The particle *-lah*: a softener with no English equivalent
body: This is your first real piece of Malay grammar. *-lah* is tacked onto a word to change the tone of the whole sentence, and in everyday Malay it is everywhere.
It doesn't have one job but four — and tone of voice decides which, much as English uses "just", "of course" or a friendly "go on":

head: Use
Malay example
Feels like
rows: Go on, give it a try.

after: How to write it: *-lah* is **attached** to the word before it, with no space and no hyphen — *duduklah*, *mestilah*, *patutlah*, *baiklah*.

⚠️ The real danger isn't misusing it but **overusing** it. Learners often stick *-lah* on every sentence because it feels "very Malay", and the result sounds like an imitation. One *-lah* every three or four sentences is plenty.

sections.title: Greeting by time of day and closeness

blocks.text: Malay uses time-of-day greetings a lot, especially in formal situations and in shops. Each covers a slightly different stretch of the day than its English counterpart:

head: Greeting
Time
Note
rows: A greeting ("good evening"), not a goodbye.

blocks.text: The word **petang** is a classic source of confusion: to a Malaysian, three o'clock is already *petang*. (In Indonesian, *petang* means dusk, so even Indonesians get caught out.) If someone suggests *jumpa petang nanti* ("see you this afternoon"), ask what time.
In casual situations Malaysians use short greetings, just like English speakers:

items: **Hai** / **helo** — to anyone, any time; always safe.
**Assalamualaikum** — to Muslims; the reply is *Waalaikumsalam*. In Malaysia this greeting is used very widely, including to open phone calls, meetings and TV broadcasts.
**Salam sejahtera** — a non-religious version, used in formal speeches and to non-Muslims.
**Apa khabar?** — a greeting and a question at once; the answer is *khabar baik*.

blocks.title: Saying goodbye
items: **Jumpa lagi** — see you again. The most common, safe anywhere.
**Selamat tinggal** — said to the person **staying behind** ("safe staying").
**Selamat jalan** — said to the person **leaving** ("safe journey").
**Bye** — widely used and doesn't feel foreign at all.
**Jaga diri** — "take care of yourself", warm and polite.

blocks.text: Malay introductions follow English word order closely, minus the verb "to be" — Malay simply leaves it out:
What needs care isn't word order but **which word for "you" and "I"** you choose. Malay has three levels, and choosing wrong feels sharper than in English:

head: Pronoun
To whom
Risk if wrong
rows: None. When in doubt, use this.
friends, people your age, fellow students
Too familiar for older people or officials.
In conversation it sounds like a bank ad.

blocks.text: The most useful Malaysian habit to copy: with people you don't know, **the word "you" is often dropped altogether** and replaced with a title. Not *Awak nak ke mana?* but *Encik nak ke mana?* ("Where is sir going?"); not *Awak jual apa?* but *Bang, jual apa?* ("Brother, what are you selling?"). It's like saying "sir" or "ma'am" — only far more often.

blocks.title: Lifesaver phrases for unit 1
items: **Maaf, saya tak faham.** — Sorry, I don't understand.
**Boleh cakap perlahan sikit?** — Could you speak a bit more slowly? (*cakap* = speak)
**Apa maksudnya?** — What does it mean?
**Saya baru belajar bahasa Melayu.** — I've just started learning Malay. This sentence opens doors anywhere; Malaysians are almost always happy to slow down.
